newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels capture key city of Kisangani.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels capture key city of Kisangani.

text.p: Rebels captured Zaire's third largest city of Kisangani on Saturday, dealing a severe blow to the government of President Mobutu Seke Seko.

"The military commander at the front said the town was liberated at 1445 (1245 GMT). He said the enemy had crossed the river and we are looking for boats so that we can pursue them," rebel leader Laurent Kabila told a news conference in the eastern town of Goma.
Kisangani residents contacted from Kinshasa confirmed the fall of the city, the army's headquarters for operations in the war zone. They said Zaire soldiers fled late on Friday and early on Saturday.
"They left this morning and last night after looting what they could in the short space of time that they had," one resident told Reuters.
Another resident said small groups of rebels had gathered in the city centre and that residents were coming out to welcome them.
Before announcing the fall of the city, Kabila had talks with United Nations envoy Mohammed Sahnoun in Goma. Sahnoun is trying to mediate an end to the fighting.

The fall of Kisangani is the biggest setback for the government since the rebels took up arms in October, vowing to topple absent and ailing Mobuto. They now hold up to a fifth of the sprawling nation.
Diplomats said resistance apparently crumbled after soldiers of Zaire's notoriously undisciplined army went on a looting spree in the city and then fled across the Zaire River.

"What happened looks distinctly like a betrayal," a senior government official said, commenting on fighting between Serb mercenaries and soldiers at the international airport on the outskirts of Kisangani late on Friday.
"The international airport has been taken and fighting is continuing in town," rebel spokesman Raphael Ngenda said in Goma earlier in the day.

France sent a plane with an escort of 30 paratroops from its base in neighbouring Central African Republic to Kisangani and successfully airlifted out 15 foreign nationals. Aid sources said it used a second smaller airport, almost in town.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe ruled out any unlateral military intervention by France, which has been lobbying unsuccessfully for a multi-national force to be sent to help aid get to refugees. Critics say its aim is to prop up Mobutu.
"We do not intend to launch again a solely French operation, and, after all, we do not have all the means to carry it out either," Juppe told a French television network.
Some diplomats said the much-heralded battle for Kisangani, a major port on the Zaire River, began after soldiers switched sides and clashed with mercenaries at the airport.
"There were clashes on the road from the airport when the mercenaries were trying to flee," one senior diplomat said. It was unclear how many of the 300 mercenaries escaped.
The rebels accuse Zaire of denying them citizenship and preparing to expel them to Rwanda, their ancestral home.
Zaire accuses neighbouring Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi of invading in support of the rebels. All three deny the charge.
The government has accepted a U.N. ceasefire plan. The rebels have resisted diplomatic pressure for a ceasefire.
Mobutu has been out of the country for most of the time since August when he had prostate cancer surgery in Europe.
